clues: A thick, white, cheesy biofilm that coats the fetal skin beginning around weeks 17 to 20.
It is composed of lipid-rich sebum secreted by fetal sebaceous glands mixed with desquamated periderm cells.
It protects the developing epidermis against maceration from continuous immersion in amniotic fluid.
A classic clinical milestone in pregnancy typically experienced between weeks 17 and 20.
It occurs earlier in multiparous women than in first-time mothers.
It represents the mother's first subjective perception of active fetal limb movements.
The specialized, glycogen- and lipid-rich functional endometrium situated directly beneath the implanting conceptus.
It forms the maternal half of the definitive placenta.
Absence of this layer allows chorionic villi to attach directly to the myometrium in placenta accreta.
One of 15 to 20 rounded, bulging lobules visible on the maternal surface of a delivered placenta.
Each lobule is separated from its neighbors by decidual septa and receives blood from maternal spiral arteries.
Retention of even one of these lobules after delivery causes severe postpartum hemorrhage.
An obstetric condition defined by a markedly reduced amniotic fluid volume (amniotic fluid index under 5 cm).
It is classically caused by fetal bilateral renal agenesis, posterior urethral valves, or preterm membrane rupture.
When severe and prolonged, it leads to Potter sequence and fatal pulmonary hypoplasia.
An intrahepatic fetal vascular shunt connecting the left umbilical vein directly to the inferior vena cava.
It allows oxygenated placental blood to bypass the hepatic capillary sinusoids.
After birth, it obliterates to form the ligamentum venosum of the liver.
A muscular fetal vessel derived from the distal left sixth aortic arch connecting the pulmonary trunk to the proximal descending aorta.
It diverts right ventricular blood away from the high-resistance fetal lungs into the systemic circulation.
Rising oxygen tension and falling prostaglandin E2 at birth cause it to close into the ligamentum arteriosum.
